Comment on Proposed Rule RIN 2900-AS31 (Supplemental Submission)

I respectfully submit this supplemental comment to emphasize two points:

1. Military Sexual Trauma (MST).
Nearly 40% of women veterans report experiencing MST during service. Forcing survivors of rape or incest to carry a pregnancy is a direct betrayal of VA’s commitment to trauma-informed care. Eliminating exceptions for rape and incest would retraumatize survivors and undermine trust in the VA system that is meant to serve them.

2. Taxpayer Costs.
While I oppose taxpayer funding of elective abortion services, I recognize that denying medically necessary care increases—not decreases—government costs. Delayed treatment for non-viable pregnancies, septic miscarriages, or life-threatening conditions leads to longer hospital stays, permanent disabilities, and higher long-term expenses to the VA healthcare system. Targeted exceptions are fiscally responsible because they prevent these costly emergencies.

For these reasons, I urge the VA to preserve coverage in cases of rape, incest, life- or health-endangering conditions, and miscarriage/ectopic care. Doing so protects MST survivors while also protecting taxpayers from avoidable future costs.

Respectfully submitted,
Michael K. Harris Sr.

Supplemental Evidence ‒ RIN 2900-AS31 Public Comment
This supplemental appendix focuses on two specific issues: (1) the prevalence and impact of Military
Sexual Trauma (MST) among veterans, and (2) the taxpayer costs associated with denying medically
necessary pregnancy care. These points are provided to reinforce my supplemental comment
submission.
Military Sexual Trauma (MST)
• Meta-analyses show approximately 38% of women veterans report experiencing MST, including
sexual harassment and assault during service (Kimerling et al., 2007; Wilson, 2019).
• VA clinical guidance emphasizes the need for trauma-informed care for MST survivors, including
sensitive handling of reproductive healthcare (VA MST Fact Sheet, 2023).
• Denying pregnancy termination options in MST-related cases increases psychological harm and
undermines survivor trust in VA services.
Taxpayer Costs of Denied Care
• Delayed treatment of miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy leads to more severe complications, longer
hospital stays, and permanent injuries̶raising costs to the VA system (KFF 2023; JAMA Network
Open 2023).
• A University of Maryland/Colorado analysis (2024) showed states with abortion bans saw increased
maternal morbidity and infant mortality, both of which carry higher healthcare costs.
• The Turnaway Study and NBER analyses found that abortion denial increases long-term economic
instability for women and families, which often shifts costs to public safety-net programs.
• Preventing medical crises with clear exceptions is less costly to taxpayers than responding to
emergencies after denial of timely care.
